content: A protein precursor, also referred to as a pro-protein or pro-peptide, is an inactive form of a protein or peptide that can be converted into its active form through post-translational modifications. The name of a protein precursor is often prefixed with pro. Examples of such precursors include proinsulin and proopiomelanocortin. Protein precursors are frequently utilized by organisms when the resulting active protein has the potential to be harmful but must be readily available in large quantities or on short notice. Enzyme precursors, specifically, are known as zymogens or proenzymes. Examples of these include enzymes found in the human digestive tract. Some protein precursors are secreted from the cell. Many of these precursors are synthesized with an N-terminal signal peptide, which directs them for secretion. Proteins containing a signal peptide are named with the prefix pre, and when combined with the pro prefix, they are referred to as pre-pro-proteins or pre-pro-peptides. The signal peptide is cleaved off in the endoplasmic reticulum during the process of protein maturation.
